nameStory: This beetle gets its "black-collared" name from the distinctive dark band that wraps around its neck region like a fancy collar on a formal shirt. The "click" part comes from its amazing ability to snap its body segments together to flip itself upright when stuck on its back, making an audible clicking sound that you can actually hear!
description: The Black-collared Click Beetle is a slender, elongated beetle about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long. Its body has a distinctive two-toned appearance with a dark blackish-brown "collar" around the thorax (the middle section behind the head) and lighter reddish-brown wing covers. Like all click beetles, it has a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body and relatively short legs tucked close to its sides.

idTips.label: Dark collar marking
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive blackish-brown band around the thorax that contrasts sharply with the lighter reddish-brown wing covers - this collar marking is usually quite prominent and feels smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Clicking behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed or placed on its back, it will arch its body and snap with an audible 'click' to flip itself over - you can gently encourage this behavior by placing it upside down on your palm

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Measures about 12-18mm long with a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body that feels firm and slightly flattened when held between your fingers

idTips.label: Surface texture
idTips.description: The wing covers have a subtle matte finish with very fine punctures that create a slightly rough texture, unlike the shinier surface of many other beetles

idTips.label: Antennae shape
idTips.description: Sports thread-like antennae that are neither clubbed nor saw-toothed, and can be tucked into grooves along the sides of the body when the beetle plays dead

habitat: Black-collared Click Beetles are found in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with decaying logs, stumps, and leaf litter. They're often discovered under loose bark of dead or dying hardwood trees like oak, maple, and birch, where their larvae develop by feeding on decaying wood.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active in late spring, emerging from their overwintering sites. This is when you're most likely to find them crawling on tree bark or flying toward lights in the evening.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly encountered. Look for them on warm evenings around porch lights or during the day when moving logs and bark.
seasonality.fall: Adults begin seeking overwintering shelter under bark, in crevices, and in leaf litter. Activity slows considerably as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults remain hidden and inactive in protected spots like deep bark crevices or under logs. Rarely seen unless you're doing serious log rolling on warmer winter days.

funFact: Click beetle larvae, called wireworms, can live up to 5 years underground before becoming adults - that's longer than many mammals live, and some of the wireworms you find today started developing when you were in a completely different grade in school!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other click beetles in the Ampedus genus, but the Black-collared is the only one with such a pronounced dark collar contrasting against lighter wing covers. Remember: "Black collar, easy holler" - if you can clearly see that dark neck band, you've got your ID.
contextualKnowledge: The family name "Elateridae" comes from the Greek word "elater" meaning "driver" or "striker," referring to their clicking mechanism. Despite being called "click beetles," many people know them better as the parents of wireworms, which can be garden pests, though the adults themselves are actually beneficial decomposers.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ampedus species commonly found in New England, compare it to other click beetles in the region by looking for that signature dark collar marking. Other click beetles might be similar in size and shape, but none have such a distinct black "necklace" around the thorax combined with the reddish-brown wing covers.
